phases.title: 1 · Preflight
phases.lede: Before the flight in earnest: nav data, a flight plan, the load and the charts. Some of these tools need the aircraft powered.

frag.v: MSFS updates its AIRAC cycle with the sim's regular updates. If your planning tool used an older cycle, the import shows errors such as
NOT IN DATABASE
and
AWY/WPT Mismatch
, or fails outright. A Navigraph subscription adds their nav data to MSFS, keeps it current, and pairs it with SimBrief.

condition.v: MFD, once the aircraft has power

action.v: its AIRAC cycle to the sim's

frag.v: Plan on
SimBrief
, not the built-in MSFS flight planner (World Map). Other planners work, but they often lack the current AIRAC cycle, and only SimBrief has the import below.
Little Nav Map
covers planning and charts,
ChartFox
covers charts, and
Navigraph
covers both, by subscription.
The FMS imports the SimBrief flight plan, as the real aircraft does from its airline. The flyPad uses the same plan to show the OFP and to import fuel and payload. FlyByWire's
SimBrief A380X Features
guide covers both.
Typing the route in by hand, and the discontinuities that appear as you do, are covered in
3 · Preparing the FMS
. Discontinuities are intended, not a fault.
The aircraft loads its own fuel, passengers and baggage. FlyByWire's
Fuel and Weights
guide has the advisories.

condition.v: flyPad; en route charts for the flight

phases.title: 2 · Cockpit Preparation
phases.lede: Cold and dark at the gate to a powered, prepared cockpit.

frag.v: Every switch should already be in its position before anything gets power. Set the parking brake; the rest you are confirming, not changing.
The batteries come first. External power then feeds the systems while the engines are off, and the aircraft needs at least two external power units to power the whole electrical network.

condition.v: BAT 1, ESS BAT, BAT 2, APU BAT; the guide's ON

frag.v: The fire tests prove the detection and extinguishing systems work. The APU then supplies power and bleed air while the engines are off. The radios go on now in case of an emergency.

condition.v: chime, warning lights and ECAM all respond
in hot weather to cut the APU load

frag.v: A good fire test gives a constant repetitive chime and a flashing
MASTER WARN
light. The ECAM shows
ENG 1(2)(3)(4) FIRE
APU FIRE
and
MLG BAY FIRE
. Every engine and APU fire pushbutton lights red, the agent pushbuttons show
SQUIB
and
DISCH
, and the fire lights on the engine master panel come on.
The SD APU page comes up on its own when the APU starts, and switches back to the previous page once the APU is running.

The flow starts at the bottom left of the overhead panel and works up, then right. It carries on down the main panel to the pedestal, programs the FMS, and finishes on the glareshield and the lateral consoles. Two pilots normally share it; alone in the sim, you do it all.

items.v: Overhead panel, left to right and bottom to top: prepare.

frag.v: Scan from left to right and bottom to top, so every switch ends up in the right position.

condition.v: as early as possible; alignment takes time

frag.v: Do a full alignment on the first flight of the day, after a crew change, when GPS is not available on every segment of the flight, or when you expect long segments with little NAVAID coverage. A fast alignment covers every other case.

condition.v: not with a high-pressure ground air unit connected

action.tip: PURSer SELection — cabin temperature set from the cabin crew panel

frag.v: A connected high-pressure ground air unit shows as pressure in the bleed system on the
SD BLEED page
. With no passenger number in the FMS, the air flow is set as if every seat were full; enter
PAX NBR
and it adjusts to match.

Get the IFR clearance before departing, from clearance delivery or the frequency the airport uses. It usually gives the destination and route, the initial altitude, the SID or radar vectors, the departure runway, the squawk and the departure frequency. Read it back, or acknowledge it in the built-in ATC menu. The
CRAFT mnemonic
) helps.

phases.title: 3 · Preparing the FMS
phases.lede: INIT, the flight plan, navaids, fuel and load, then takeoff performance. The Source column carries the guide's sample flight, Munich (EDDM) to Frankfurt (EDDF); use your own OFP's values.

frag.v: The MFD runs entirely on mouse and keyboard. Buttons are grey boxes: a downward triangle marks a dropdown, greyed-out text marks a disabled button, and tabs are buttons too. The mouse pointer is a yellow
X
with a dot in the middle, and a selected button or field gets a blue border. Click a field for a blue typing cursor, type on your keyboard, and press
ENTER
to confirm.
The start-up page also shows the aircraft and engine type, the nav database serial number, and the pilot-stored waypoints, routes, navaids and runways.
The flight number, the airports, the cruise level, the cost index and the route are the basis the FMS manages the flight from.

TOGA gives full thrust for short runways or adverse conditions. FLEX reduces thrust against an assumed higher temperature, which lowers engine stress and saves fuel. The guide takes off on FLEX.
The

gives the numbers.

phases.title: 4 · Engine Start and Taxi
phases.lede: Pushback and engine start to the runway holding point.

frag.v: Start this once the passengers are boarded and the aircraft is secure. You need the IFR clearance, and the APU running with
AVAIL
showing.

items.full: doors, jet bridge, Ground Power Unit and ground equipment

action.v: check the low pressure ground carts

frag.v: Ground power comes off before the push so the ground crew can unplug it. The low pressure carts go too: left connected during the start, they can cause faulty triggers.
Call ground and tell them you are ready to push and start. They clear you onto a taxiway and give you a direction to face:
Callsign
, Ground. You are clear to push and start onto Whiskey 3 facing north.
Request pushback clearance:
ATC Communications › Ground

The checklists live on the EWD. Press C/L on the ECAM control panel to open them, move with the UP and DOWN keys, and tick an item with the check-mark key. The aircraft senses some items itself and ticks them for you, BEACON among them.

action.v: control buttons or the rudder and elevator

frag.v: Some stands never show a tug. The pushback still works, and it looks like an invisible tug is pushing you. MSFS ATC and third-party add-ons can push you too; this guide uses the flyPad.
Wait until you are clear of the terminal, or the ground crew has told you it is clear to start.

condition.v: the SD ENG page appears; wait 10 s for the engine tests
two-engine taxi: the other pair, started on the way to the runway

frag.v: A started engine shows
AVAIL
and settles at roughly
4.2 % THR
367 °C EGT
and
670 kg/h FF
Any engine can go first, at the pilot's discretion; the guide starts 1, 2, 3, then 4. The engines need bleed air to start, so the APU must be available with
APU BLEED

on, as set in cockpit preparation. A Ground Air Starter Unit, connected from the flyPad Ground Services page, also works. Crossbleed from a running engine is for starting the rest during a reduced-engine taxi. FlyByWire's
Crossbleed Engine Start
guide covers it, and the A380 procedure is similar.

condition.v: icing expected, or water, slush, ice or snow on the ground, below 10 °C OAT
for the guide's flight, from T.O PERF

action.tip: Nose Wheel STEERING DISConnected — the towing memo

frag.v: Do it with the flaps at the takeoff setting. Work pitch, then roll, then yaw, holding each input long enough for the surfaces to reach full travel.

action.tip: rudder PEDAL DISConnect — the tiller's centre button

condition.v: takes nosewheel steering off the pedals
two-engine taxi: wait until all four run

frag.v: Have the airport chart or diagram open before you move. Read back the taxi clearance first:
Callsign
, Ground. Runway 08L, taxi via Whiskey 2, hold short of November 3,
> continue via November to Alpha 3, hold short Alpha 3.
Request taxi:
ATC Communications › Ground

action.tip: PLAN — the north-up, flight-plan ND mode

condition.v: add a little to get going when heavy
press the pedals smoothly and release; not in a turn

frag.v: Keep
in a straight line: past that, brake back to 10 kt and let it accelerate again. Slow to
for a sharp turn, and expect to need a little more thrust if one comes straight away.

The aircraft needs little power. Even heavy and taxiing uphill it takes no more than 10 % of the engine thrust, and too much damages airport signs. If you need more, add it on the outer engines so the inner ones ingest less debris. Ground idle runs higher with engine anti-ice on.
Skipped as INOP in the A380X: TAXI (ETACS), "currently not available or possible to implement in the simulator", and the camera of RWY TURN OFF & CAMERA, for the same reason.
Taxi only on taxiways wide enough for the A380's wingspan, which in practice means large international airports such as EGLL, EDDF or KJFK. Some publish a separate A380 taxi chart.
A two-engine taxi has to use a symmetrical pair:
on the outer engines or

on the inner ones. Pick 2+3 where the turns are tight, to cut the chance of ingesting debris. Run the after start steps for that pair, and hold the AFTER START checklist until all four engines are running.

condition.v: keep the line on the grey bar between the PFD and ND

frag.v: Check the FMS as you go, and again if the clearance changes on the way out. Alone in the sim, do it stopped at the holding point, clear of the taxiway if you are on online ATC.

condition.v: the guide's BEFORE TAKEOFF, down to the line

frag.v: Never cross a runway, active or not, without an explicit clearance from ATC and a readback.
If MSFS started you on the runway, the FMS and AFS still have to be set up as in the earlier phases. Then skip to Takeoff.

If you come from other airliners, note that the sidestick commands the flight control computers, not the surfaces, and autotrim holds the pitch whenever you let go, autopilot or not. Autothrust never moves the thrust levers. They set the most power it may use, and after takeoff they stay in the CL detent. On the AFS control panel, push a knob for managed mode and pull it for selected; dashes in the SPD or HDG window mean managed. In MSFS, clicking a knob up pushes it and clicking it down pulls it. The flight phases run preflight, takeoff, climb, cruise, descent, approach, go around and done, and the flight envelope protections make a stall or overspeed close to impossible.
You are holding short with the parking brake set, usually now on the Tower frequency:
ATC Communications › Tower

The taxi and runway turn off lights switch off by themselves when the gear retracts. Move the switches to OFF anyway.
This is usually the moment to check in with Departure:
ATC Communications › Departure
. Without a higher clearance the autopilot levels off at the selected altitude.

Climb in CLB or OP CLB, not V/S. V/S guidance outranks speed guidance, so a rate the aircraft cannot hold makes it speed up or slow down until the speed limit is reached, and only then does the V/S give way.
The climb to the cruise level usually comes in steps, each cleared by ATC. The autopilot holds the selected or managed speed and manages the thrust.
The aircraft accelerates to the climb speed on the PERF CLB page.

frag.v: The transition altitude depends on the country: 18,000 ft in the U.S., 3000 ft in the Netherlands. Standard is 29.92 inHg or 1013 hPa.

on a direct-to a waypoint in the plan
not in the plan: DIR TO button, bottom right of F-PLN

frag.v: Start descent planning
from the destination.

The arrival mirrors the departure. A STAR leads from the last en-route waypoint to the initial approach fix, with levels, speed limits and often a clearance limit you may not pass without ATC, holding there if you must. The instrument approach takes you on to the final approach fix, though with light traffic, and on online networks especially, ATC often vectors you straight there. The ILS then guides you down: the localizer laterally, the glideslope vertically. Fly from real charts, not MSFS's planner. Navigraph is built into the flyPad, and ChartFox is free with a VATSIM account.
Start about
200 NM

out, and on a short flight before the flight. Descent planning is the pilot's job, not ATC's. They will often give descent instructions, but you must know where your top of descent is and ask for the clearance if it has not come.
What drives the plan: the cruise level, the STAR's altitude constraints, its speed constraints, since slowing down while descending is hard, and passenger comfort.

condition.v: a STAR waypoint, the FAF altitude, or the field elevation
F-PLN: press the waypoint, then DIR TO

frag.v: Treat the STAR and approach as optional. ATC may vector you to a different runway or shortcut the arrival, but only if you are low enough by then.
Rule of thumb, without the flyPad:
distance = altitude difference × 3 ÷ 1000, plus about 10 % margin

. FL320 down to FL140 is 18,000 ft, so 54 NM, so about 59 NM. Take less margin into a headwind and more with a tailwind. The later descents in a STAR are usually designed for a 3° path and need less planning, and ATC will often assign levels that differ from the chart.
DIR TO is the only way to read the distance to a waypoint short of adding up the legs on the F-PLN page. The ND distance rings can show it too.

About 50 NM before the descent, reconfirm the landing runway and fill in PERF APPR. QNH, temperature, magnetic wind and transition level come from the destination ATIS; the minima come from the approach chart.

condition.v: CAT I: the DA or MDA, 528 for the guide's EDDF 07C
CAT II/III: the RA or DH

frag.v: The A380 is CAT IIIB capable with autoland and approach category C, but the guide lands by hand, so it uses CAT I BARO minima. BARO is barometric altitude; RADIO is radio altitude above the ground.

MSFS's built-in ATC only offers the destination ATIS once you are close; on an online network you can request it now. If the chart gives the transition level as "By ATC" and you are offline, use the real-world D-ATIS, or the transition altitude plus 1000 ft. A SimBrief import fills it in for you.

Skipped as INOP in the A380X: the landing performance check, since "there is no landing performance calculator for the A380X yet"; FIX INFO, which the A380X "does not yet have implemented"; and the weather radar at 20,000 ft, "currently not available in the A380X".
Insert the APPR, STAR, TRANS and APPR VIA if they are not in the active flight plan yet.

items.full: runway, approach, via, Standard Terminal Arrival Route and transition selection

frag.v: If available, set up the airport map and brake to vacate for the destination. OANS draws the airport on the ND at range ZOOM. BTV picks the runway exit and brakes to make it.

action.tip: PLAN — the north-up, flight-plan ND mode

condition.v: after the wet line; mind the gate and turnaround time
on a short one or without BTV

frag.v: Autobrake gives even brake pressure and keeps the brakes from overheating. Pick the mode for the weight, runway length, conditions and wind. For BTV, set the mode before you take the airport map off the ND.
A few minutes before the calculated TOD, ask for the descent if ATC has not already given it:
ATC Communications › Request descent
Do not start down without a clearance.
The A380 draws a downward arrow at its own TOD, but the number remains yours to validate.

Managed descent (DES) keeps the constraints; it flies a computed vertical profile and can give very high and very low vertical speeds. Selected descent (OP DES) ignores the constraints and gives the steady descent most people expect, so start with it if DES is new to you.

ATC rarely clears you all the way down at once, and still expects the STAR's constraints to be met under a lower clearance. Managed descent handles this: it levels off at a constraint and continues once it no longer applies. Otherwise descend only to the constraint, and repeat.
Avoid V/S. Its guidance outranks speed guidance, so a rate the aircraft cannot hold makes it speed up or slow down until the speed limit is reached.
Some airline SOPs order the next steps differently.

In real life the cabin crew are asked to prepare the cabin during the descent, mostly when the seat belt signs come on. They answer with the CABIN READY call once they are strapped in themselves, usually by final approach.
Laterally this is just more flight plan: let the autopilot fly it, and set the altitude and speed to the chart or to ATC. Expect to be handed to Approach:
ATC Communications › Approach
. Expect vectors off the published route too, for separation in heavy traffic or as a shortcut when there is none, until you intercept the localizer.

Approach's last instruction is usually to call Tower once established on the localizer.

frag.v: Check in with Tower,
ATC Communications › Tower (Landing)
. Their clearance for the ILS approach is the clearance to descend on the glideslope.
APPR

arms the glideslope as well, so the aircraft will start down the moment it captures. Do not descend without a clearance, and only when directly on the localizer path, where obstacle clearance is guaranteed. To split the two, press

In APPR phase with managed speed, the aircraft targets S speed after FLAPS 1, F speed after FLAPS 2, and V
app
once the landing flap is selected. Aim to be in CONF 1 at S speed by the time FLAPS 2 is due, before the glideslope intercept.

If ATC assigns a speed ("160 kt until 5 NM"), pull the

knob for selected speed until that point, then push back to managed and take the gear, FLAPS 3 and FLAPS FULL from there.

With FLAPS 2 set, check the aircraft is decelerating toward F speed. If the glideslope intercept is below 2,000 ft above the ground, set FLAPS 2 at one dot below the glideslope. Above the glideslope, or not slowing down, extend the landing gear. The speed brakes do little at low speed.

above the ground.

phases.title: 8 · After Landing and Taxi to Gate
phases.short: After Landing and Taxi to Gate
phases.lede: Runway vacated, stopped on the taxiway, to the gate.

frag.v: Tower has been told the runway is vacated. Flaps and ground spoilers are still out. Tower usually hands you to Ground, who gives the taxi instructions. Write them down and read them back, but do not start moving until the after-landing tasks are done unless ATC says so; online controllers expect them to take a moment.

items.v: AUTO fires the strobes once the main gear strut is no longer compressed, so they stay dark on the ground. Set ON for the takeoff roll and whenever you cross a runway. After landing the guide sets AUTO, and OFF once across a runway on the way in.
on before pushback, off once N1 is below 5 % on all four engines. It tells the ground crew the engines are about to start or still running.
on with power, off when securing the aircraft. With NAV on and the aircraft on the ground, the white obstruction lights on the wing tips come on too.
has no row: it is INOP in the A380X. On the real aircraft its AUTO position lights the tail logo on the ground, and in flight with the slats out.
sit on the nose gear strut and switch off by themselves when the gear retracts. Move the switches to OFF anyway. NOSE at T.O lights the taxi and takeoff lights, at TAXI the taxi lights only.
is printed RWY TURN OFF & CAMERA. The camera lights come on only with the taxi cameras (ETACS), which are INOP, so the switch works the runway turn off lights alone.
is ON or OFF. Off above 10,000 ft in the climb, on again by 10,000 ft in the descent.
lights the wing leading edges and the engine intakes, to check for ice.

off above 10,000 ft only once stable: good weather, no planned turns. Back on by 10,000 ft in the descent. Its AUTO position, which the guide does not use, lights the signs with the engines running and the slats or gear extended.

takes the place of a NO SMOKING sign, which the A380 does not have; the guide's NO SMOKING at shutdown means this selector. At AUTO the signs come on below about 13,000 ft AGL, or over a country that bans mobile phones.
at ARM lights the emergency lighting if normal electrical power fails. At OFF, an amber OFF light shows on the selector.
stands for the pedestal cockpit lighting knobs: INTEG LT, MAIN PNL FLOOD LT, PEDESTAL FLOOD LT and AMBIENT LT, each from OFF to BRT.
is the knobs under the glareshield.

head: V-Speed
Term
rows: - The highest speed (V) during take-off that you can reject the takeoff and still stop on the runway. — The lowest speed from which a takeoff can be safely continued within the takeoff distance after an engine failure at the critical engine failure speed.
Takeoff safety speed (V) the aircraft attains no later than an altitude of 35 ft (11 m) and is maintained during the 2nd segment of takeoff with one engine failed.
The maximum speed (V) at which a full control deflection in one direction should be made in normal or alternate law.
Speed (V) for flying down the approach.
Maximum structural design limit speed (V) and Mach.
Predictive VFE at next flap/slat position.
Maximum gear Extension speed (V), often lower than the operating speed to prevent gear door damage.
Maximum gear Operating speed (V), which means the max speed for the gear being down.
Airbus for the MAXimum speed (V) for the current configuration, represented by a black and red strip at the top of the airspeed indication.
Minimum speed (V) in the Air that if one engine fails and the other is at TO thrust, you can still control the aircraft with the primary flight controls up to a bank of 5 degrees.
Minimum speed (V) on the Ground that if one engine fails and the other is at TO thrust, you can still control the aircraft with the primary flight controls.
Maximum Operating speed (V), also has MMO for maximum Mach number.
Rotate speed (V). The speed at which the pilot pulls back on the stick to pitch the airplane to the takeoff attitude.
REFerence speed (V) for a normal approach at the 50-foot height.
Stalling speed (V) at which airplane is controllable.
Stalling speed (V) or minimum steady flight speed obtained in a specified configuration.
Stalling speed (V) or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration.
Airbus for when the Stall Warning will activate, represented by a black and red strip at the bottom of the airspeed indicator, when there has been a failure to affect the flight control laws.
Speed (V) for best angle of climb.
Speed (V) for best rate of climb.
Airbus speed (V) for the MAXimum angle of attack (α) that the pilot can achieve in normal law, shown by the top of a red strip at the bottom of the airspeed indicator.

Airbus for the speed (V) that the angle of attack (α) PROTection will become active to stop the aircraft from stalling, shown as being the top of the black and amber strip at the bottom of the airspeed indicator.

head: V-Speed
Term
rows: Minimum speed at which the Flaps may be retracted at takeoff (i.e., CONF 2/3). Also, the minimum speed in approach when in CONF 2 or 3
Minimum speed at which the Slats may be retracted at takeoff. Also, the minimum speed in approach when in CONF 1.
Green Dot speed, engine-out Operating speed with flaps up, best lift-to-drag ratio speed, also corresponds to final takeoff speed.
